## NHS Waiting Times Under the Spotlight


Access to timely healthcare remains one of the biggest concerns for patients across England. While the National Health Service (NHS) continues to provide care to millions of people every year, significant differences exist in waiting times depending on where patients receive treatment.


Recent analysis of NHS England data has highlighted major variations in hospital performance, revealing which NHS trusts are providing faster treatment and which are struggling to meet national targets. The findings also shed light on the growing issue of last-minute operation cancellations and delays in rescheduling procedures.


For patients waiting for specialist treatment, surgery, or diagnostic services, understanding these differences can help provide insight into the challenges facing healthcare services across the country.


## What Is the NHS 18-Week Treatment Target?


The NHS has a long-standing commitment to begin treatment for most patients within 18 weeks of referral by a GP or another healthcare professional. Officially, the NHS aims for 92% of patients to start treatment within this timeframe.


However, this target has not been achieved nationally for several years due to rising demand, workforce pressures, and increased pressure on hospital resources.


Despite these challenges, recent data suggests some improvement. Nationally, 65.8% of patients on NHS waiting lists had been waiting 18 weeks or less by September 2026, representing the highest proportion recorded since September 2021.


Even so, the national average hides significant regional differences.


## Hospitals With the Shortest Waiting Times


Several NHS trusts are performing considerably better than the national average when it comes to managing patient waiting lists.


### 1. Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust


Moorfields Eye Hospital emerged as one of the strongest-performing trusts in England. According to the data, 85.6% of patients awaiting treatment were still within the 18-week target period.


This means only a relatively small proportion of patients experienced delays beyond the recommended waiting time.


### 2. Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust


Northumbria Healthcare also demonstrated strong performance, with 83.6% of patients being treated within the target timeframe.


The trust, which operates facilities including Northumbria Specialist Emergency Care Hospital, continues to be recognised for its efficient service delivery.


### 3. Royal Berkshire NHS Foundation Trust


Royal Berkshire NHS Foundation Trust ranked among the best-performing providers, with 82.7% of patients remaining within the 18-week treatment window.


Its performance stood out not only for waiting times but also for its management of cancelled procedures.


## Hospitals Facing the Longest Delays


While some trusts are delivering care within recommended timeframes, others continue to struggle with large waiting lists and extended delays.


### Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust


Mid and South Essex recorded the lowest performance level in the analysis. Only 51.6% of patients had been waiting for less than 18 weeks.


In practical terms, almost half of all patients awaiting treatment had already exceeded the national target.


The trust operates major facilities including Basildon University Hospital, Broomfield Hospital, and Southend University Hospital.


### University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust


University Hospitals Sussex ranked among the poorest performers, with only 52% of patients remaining within the 18-week target period.


The trust manages several major hospital sites, including Royal Sussex County Hospital and Worthing Hospital.


### Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust


Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust also experienced substantial delays, with just 54.7% of patients being treated within the recommended timeframe.


These figures demonstrate the significant variation that patients may encounter depending on where they access NHS services.


## The Growing Issue of Cancelled Operations


Another key concern highlighted by the data is the number of elective operations that are cancelled at short notice.


Last-minute cancellations can occur for several reasons, including:


- Staff shortages
- Lack of available hospital beds
- Limited operating theatre capacity
- Unexpected surges in emergency care demand
- Patient clinical conditions preventing surgery


Under NHS policy, patients whose non-emergency operations are cancelled for non-clinical reasons should receive a replacement treatment date within 28 days.


However, compliance with this requirement varies significantly between trusts.


## Trusts With High Numbers of Delayed Rescheduling


The analysis found that some trusts recorded particularly high numbers of breaches of the 28-day rescheduling standard.


### North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust


North West Anglia reported 625 cancelled operations during the review period. Of these, 498 patients were not provided with treatment within the expected 28-day period.


This represented one of the highest breach rates identified.


### George Eliot Hospital NHS Foundation Trust


George Eliot Hospital also recorded substantial challenges in meeting the standard, with 124 breaches among 196 cancelled procedures.


### Alder Hey Children's NHS Foundation Trust


Alder Hey Children's NHS Foundation Trust recorded 117 breaches compared with 202 cancellations.


Trust representatives noted that some delays may be related to children being medically unfit for surgery at the scheduled time.


## Trusts Performing Well on Rescheduling


Not all trusts experienced difficulties.


Several organisations reported no breaches of the 28-day standard following last-minute cancellations.


These included:


- Royal United Hospitals Bath NHS Foundation Trust
- Royal Berkshire NHS Foundation Trust
- Northampton General Hospital NHS Trust


Their performance suggests that effective operational management can help minimise disruption for patients even when procedures must be cancelled.


## Why NHS Waiting Times Matter


Long waiting times can have a significant impact on patient wellbeing.


Delayed treatment may contribute to:


- Increased anxiety and stress
- Reduced quality of life
- Worsening symptoms
- Longer recovery periods
- Greater pressure on emergency healthcare services


For some medical conditions, delays may affect mobility, independence, and the ability to work or carry out everyday activities.


This is why NHS performance targets remain an important measure of healthcare quality and accessibility.


## Winter Pressures Could Create Additional Challenges


Healthcare leaders have warned that pressures are likely to increase further during the winter months.


Recent NHS figures showed that October was the busiest month ever recorded for Accident and Emergency departments, with more than 2.5 million attendances.


Ambulance services also faced exceptionally high demand, responding to nearly 870,000 incidents during the same period.


Cold weather, seasonal illnesses, respiratory infections, and increased hospital admissions traditionally place additional strain on healthcare services.


As a result, maintaining progress on waiting lists may become increasingly difficult in the months ahead.


## Looking Ahead


The latest NHS data shows that overall performance is improving compared with previous years, but significant inequalities remain across England.


While trusts such as Moorfields Eye Hospital, Northumbria Healthcare, and Royal Berkshire are demonstrating strong results, others continue to face major challenges in reducing waiting times and managing cancellations.


For patients, these findings highlight the continuing importance of investment, workforce planning, and operational efficiency within the NHS.


As demand for healthcare continues to rise, reducing geographical disparities and ensuring timely access to treatment will remain a critical priority for healthcare leaders across the country.
